account: Simeral and colleagues published a study from the BrainGate pilot trial in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering in 2021. The authors are at Brown University, Massachusetts General Hospital, Providence VA Medical Center and Stanford University. Two men with tetraplegia from C4 spinal cord injury, T5 (63) and T10 (35), used a 192-electrode intracortical brain-computer interface. Wireless transmitters replaced its cables. Sessions were in their homes. A Kalman filter decoder and a linear discriminant classifier converted neural activity into cursor velocity and clicks. Both controlled an unmodified commercial tablet to browse the web and run apps. T5 typed 196 correct characters in 14.6 minutes (13.4 per minute) in Notepad. Neural data were recorded continuously from T10 for 24 hours at home. Calendar dates are not given. Brown University announced the study on 31 March 2021. In the release, Leigh Hochberg said that home visits stopped in March 2020 because of the pandemic. He said that caregivers were then trained to set up the wireless link, so that a trial participant used the interface with no research staff present. T5 went on to type 90 characters per minute by attempted handwriting in a Nature study published on 12 May 2021.

summary: Two men with tetraplegia used a wireless BrainGate brain-computer interface at home; its decoders turned neural activity into cursor movement and clicks for browsing and typing on a tablet.
system: BrainGate wireless intracortical brain-computer interface (Kalman filter velocity decoder plus linear discriminant click classifier)
title: Two men with tetraplegia use a wireless BrainGate brain-computer interface at home to control a tablet and type
